title: Read These 3 Lines Before You Sign an Off-Plan Contract
seoTitle: 3 Lines to Read Before You Sign an Off-Plan Contract
description: You can be right about the market and still lose money on one page. Check assignment, the fee and the completion date before you sign off-plan.
answer: Before you sign an off-plan contract, read three lines with your lawyer. First, assignment: can you sell the contract before the building is finished? Second, the fee: if you can sell it, how much does the developer take? Third, the date: when is the building due, and how late can it be? keywords: what to check before signing a presale contract
body:
You can read the market perfectly and still lose money on an off-plan deal. Prices go up, the neighborhood improves, demand is there, and you still cannot collect your profit. In my experience the reason is usually not the market at all. It is one page of the contract that nobody read closely enough.

## Why one page can cost you the whole profit

When you buy off-plan, most of the money is made in the gap between the price you pay at launch and the price the unit is worth later. Many investors plan to capture that gap by selling the contract before the building is finished. That plan only works if the contract lets you do it, at a cost you can live with, within a timeline you expected.

Three lines decide all of that.

## The 3 lines to check before you sign

1. **Assignment.** Can you sell your contract to another buyer before the building is finished? Some contracts do not allow it at all. Others allow it only after a certain point, or only with the developer's approval. If your strategy is to flip, this line is everything.
2. **The fee.** If you are allowed to sell the contract, how much does the developer take when you do? A fee can eat a large part of the gain you were counting on, so you need to know the number before you run your math.
3. **The date.** When is the building due, and how late can it be? Contracts often give the developer room to delay. A longer wait means your money stays locked up longer, and your exit moves further away.

## How these lines work together

Think of it this way. The assignment line tells you if the exit door exists. The fee tells you what it costs to walk through it. The date tells you when the door opens and how long it can stay closed. Miss any one of the three, and the profit you saw on paper may never reach your pocket.

## Read it with your lawyer, before you sign

This is not something to check after the deposit is paid. Once you sign, the terms are the terms. Sit down with your lawyer, find these three lines, and make sure they match the plan you have in your head. If they do not, you either negotiate, adjust your plan, or walk away.

This is my opinion and my own practice, not legal or financial advice. But I have seen it again and again: being right about the market is not enough. You also have to be right about the contract.
takeaways: You can be right about the market and still lose money because of the contract terms.
The assignment line tells you if you can sell the contract before the building is finished.
The fee line tells you how much the developer takes when you sell the contract.
The date line tells you when the building is due and how late it is allowed to be.
Read all three lines with your lawyer before you sign, not after the deposit is paid.
faq: What is an assignment clause in an off-plan contract?

It is the part of the contract that says whether you can sell your purchase contract to another buyer before the building is finished. Some contracts allow it, some restrict it, and some do not allow it at all.
Do developers charge a fee to assign a presale contract?
Many do. The contract states how much the developer takes when you sell your contract, and that fee can reduce your profit significantly, so check it before you sign.
Can an off-plan completion date be delayed?
Yes. Contracts often allow the developer to deliver later than the target date. Check how late the building is allowed to be, because a delay keeps your money locked up longer.
Should I have a lawyer review an off-plan contract?
Yes. Go through the assignment, fee and completion date terms with your lawyer before you sign, while you can still negotiate or walk away.
